gap: No result ChatGPT got states that OptiMate's '3-5 A pulse current' for its 20 W Solar DUO is not the charge rate: TecMate's comparable figure is 1.67 A average, which is exactly 20 W ÷ 12 V and matches its 10 W (0.83 A) and 40 W (3.3 A) ratings. SUNER POWER publishes only MPPT efficiency percentages (99% tracking, 98% conversion) and no amp figure, so the 'MPPT' and 'pulse' labels cannot be compared directly. On amps per watt, the brands sit on the same panel-watts ÷ 12 V ceiling.
standout_why: I compared this against energyforthetaking.com (2026-10-27), solarbatteryscout.com and gopowersolar.com's 10W-vs-20W blog. Energyforthetaking estimates a 20 W panel at 1.2-1.4 A in peak sun and says it reports no measured or rated output. Gopowersolar gives 0.6 A for 10 W and 1.2 A for 20 W, plus a daily-Ah formula. Solarbatteryscout states no charge current for any product and says 'we haven't used these products'. Rivals therefore already give rough amps per watt. None of them sorts pulse current from average current, quotes OptiMate's 1.67 A average or its <0.5 mA night draw, or points out that SUNER's efficiency percentages come with no amp rating.
decides: This confirms the pick by panel watts and does not overturn it. A shopper choosing between 20 W units should expect about 1.67 A at most (20 W ÷ 12 V) whatever the controller label, so a 'pulse' or '99% MPPT' claim is not a reason to pay $169.95 MSRP for the OptiMate DUO 20W over SUNER's $69.99-$85.95 20 W Ultra. The real differences are other things. OptiMate states it starts charging from 4 V, draws <0.5 mA at night and detects LiFePO4 by itself. SUNER makes you choose the 12V, AGM or Lithium mode by hand.

findings.label: Rated charge current, average vs pulse
findings.note: Use the average figure when comparing. 20 W ÷ 12 V = 1.67 A, so the maker's average equals the panel-watts-over-nominal-voltage ceiling. The pulse figure is a peak inside each pulse, not sustained charging.

findings.label: Night / monitor-mode draw on the battery
findings.note: 0.5 mA × 24 h × 30 d = 0.36 Ah a month at most. For scale, gopowersolar's table lists a single LP/CO detector at 0.06 A.
